transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi doctor, thank you. Well, I guess... it's just been really frustrating lately. I work as a secretary, and I've been doing admin work since high school, so my entire day is usually about keeping things organized for other people. But what finally made me ask for help is that I just keep forgetting little things I normally handle without a problem. 

It's the small stuff, you know? Like, I'll completely forget to return calls, which is ridiculous because I'm sitting right by the phone all day. Or I had this registration form I needed to turn in, and I just... I don't know, it completely slipped my mind even though I knew it was important. And errands are a nightmare right now. I'll plan to stop for an errand on the way home, and I'll think about it all afternoon, but then I just drive straight home and pull into the driveway before I realize I drove right past the place. 

It's just so embarrassing because I'm 36 years old and I should be able to remember to pick up a few things or drop off a simple form. I try to leave myself notes, but then I just walk right past the notes without looking at them. It's making me feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit, to be honest, just constantly dropping the ball on these everyday tasks that shouldn't be this hard. So I just really felt like I needed to come in and figure out what is going on with me.
Are you experiencing these memory problems only at work or are you also forgetting things in your personal life?

Oh, it’s definitely both. It’s bleeding into everything, which is why I’m so worked up about it. I mean, I’m still getting by, you know? The house hasn't burned down and I haven't been fired. But at work, I’ve been missing these small follow-ups. Just little things, like checking if a vendor got an email or following up on a supply order. And that really, really stresses me out because I've been an admin since I was eighteen, right out of high school, and I've been working so hard because my boss and I had actually talked about me potentially moving into an Office Manager role. 

It's something I really want, to finally take that next step. But now I'm terrified that all these little slip-ups are going to completely ruin my reputation. Like, how can they promote me to manage the whole office if I can't even remember to follow up with a client like I promised? 

And then outside of work, in my personal life, it's just as bad. I mentioned the errands, but I also have these school deadlines that I keep missing. I've been taking a couple of night classes to help with that promotion, just to bolster my resume since I don't have a college degree, and you wouldn't believe how hard it is to just remember to submit an assignment on time. I'll literally do the reading, and then I just... I don't know, I forget to hit submit, or I mix up the dates entirely and realize it was due a week ago. 

It's just so frustrating because I'm trying so hard to keep all these plates spinning, and I'm so worried people are starting to look at me like I'm unreliable or careless, which isn't me at all. I've always prided myself on being the one who remembers everything for everyone else, so this is just... it's really taking a toll on my confidence, honestly. I just don't want to mess up this Office Manager opportunity over something so stupid.
Are you feeling sad, anxious, or irritable more often than usual?

Well, um... I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly. I mean, I'm definitely not walking around crying all the time or feeling like I can't get out of bed, you know? It's not like that heavy, dark feeling people talk about when they're depressed. And I wouldn't say I'm super anxious in general, like having panic attacks or worrying about everything under the sun. 

But, I mean, I *am* stressed. Really stressed. Like I was saying about the Office Manager position—it's just constantly on my mind. And when I realize I forgot something *again*, I do get this horrible sinking feeling in my stomach. It's like, "Oh great, what else have I dropped the ball on today?" So I guess there's some anxiety there, but it's very specific to me messing up at work or school. It's not like a general, free-floating anxiety. It's more of a... a dread of the consequences of my own forgetfulness. 

And as for irritable... maybe a little? But again, it's mostly directed at myself. I get so mad at myself when I walk past a note I left on the counter, or when I pull into the driveway and realize I forgot to stop at the pharmacy. I'll just sit in the car and think, "How could you be so stupid?" Sometimes I might snap a little bit if someone interrupts me when I'm trying really, really hard to focus on something so I don't forget it, but I don't think I'm walking around angry at the world. It's just... it's just this constant, underlying frustration with my own brain, you know? It's exhausting having to police yourself all the time and still failing at it. But I don't think it's like a clinical depression or anxiety thing. Just... just being really fed up with myself.
Are you having trouble remembering things related to your personal relationships, like birthdays or appointments with friends and family?

Well, birthdays and stuff... I mean, mostly it's the everyday things. Like I was saying earlier, what really pushed me to finally make an appointment and come in here was just this constant stream of forgetting all these little things I normally handle without any problem at all. 

It's just so bizarre. Like returning calls—I sit right next to a phone all day, I have a notepad right there, I'll talk to someone and say, "I'll call you right back with that information," and then... poof. It's gone from my brain until hours later. Or that registration form I mentioned. It was sitting right on my desk, I knew exactly where it was, I knew I needed to turn it in, and I just completely forgot about it. 

And the errands! Oh my gosh, the errands are the worst part right now. I'll be at work, and I'll think, "Okay, on the way home, I need to stop at the grocery store for milk, and I need to drop off the dry cleaning." I'll repeat it to myself in the car, I'll even picture the route in my head, and then I'll just go on autopilot, drive my normal route home, pull into the driveway, turn off the car, and then it hits me. I drove right past the grocery store and the dry cleaner. 

So it's really those types of daily activities. I don't know if I'm forgetting birthdays more than usual, because I've always relied on my calendar for that anyway, but it's these little daily tasks, these things I do every single day, that are just slipping right through the cracks. It's like my brain just deletes the information the second I look away.
Have you noticed any difficulty learning new things, such as new skills or information, since you started experiencing these memory problems?

No, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble learning new things, exactly. I mean, it's not like I'm sitting in my night classes and the professor is speaking Greek. When I'm actually sitting there, paying attention—well, trying to pay attention—and taking notes, the concepts make sense. Like, we're doing this module on organizational behavior right now, which is super relevant for the Office Manager thing, and I get it. I understand the theories and the case studies and all of that. 

The problem isn't the learning part, it's the... the execution part, I guess? It's like I can absorb the information just fine, but then keeping track of what I'm supposed to do with it, or when I'm supposed to do it, is where everything falls apart. Like I said, I'll do all the reading for a new topic, completely understand it, and then totally forget to actually upload the assignment by 11:59 PM. 

And at work, it's the same kind of deal. If my boss shows me a new way to format a report or a new feature in our scheduling software, I pick it up right away. I've always been a quick learner when it comes to admin stuff; you kind of have to be when you're the one holding the office together. But it's just... it's the remembering to *use* the new formatting on the report three days later, or remembering to click that one specific box in the new software when I'm rushing to get a meeting scheduled. 

So, yeah, the actual learning of new skills or facts hasn't really changed. My brain can still comprehend new things. It's just that the new things—and the old things, honestly—just don't seem to stick in my short-term memory long enough for me to actually follow through on them. It's like the filing cabinet in my head is still working, but the receptionist who's supposed to put the files in the right folders keeps going on coffee breaks and leaving the papers scattered all over the desk.
Have you experienced any major life changes or stressful events recently?

Well, major life changes... I mean, the biggest thing, the thing that really seems to be the root of all this, is school. I started this evening certificate program about 15 months ago, and honestly, that's when these attention and organization problems became noticeably harder to manage. 

Before that, I was just working. And you know, being an admin assistant, I've got my routines. I go in, I know the drill, I handle the phones, the scheduling, the filing—it's all very structured. I mean, I'm 36, I've been doing this kind of work since I got out of high school, so I have my systems in place. But then, about a year and a quarter ago, I decided I wanted to go for this Office Manager position that was going to be opening up. Our current manager is retiring, and I thought, "This is my chance, I need to step up." But they wanted someone with some formal management training, which I didn't have, just my high school diploma and years of experience. So, I enrolled in this business administration certificate program at the community college.

And it's just... it's been a lot. It's not just the classes themselves, which are two nights a week, but it's the reading, the assignments, the group projects—which, don't even get me started on group projects when you're already struggling to keep your own head above water. Trying to coordinate with three other adults who all work full-time? It's a nightmare. 

So, I'm working 8 to 5, then I'm rushing to class, or I'm rushing home to log onto a virtual lecture, and then I'm up until midnight trying to read textbook chapters on human resources law or whatever. And that's when everything really started slipping. It's like my brain was a sponge that was already full with just my day job, and now I'm trying to pour a whole bucket of water on it, and it's just spilling everywhere. The forgetting the phone calls, the leaving the registration form on my desk, driving past the grocery store—all of that really ramped up after I started the program. 

It's just this constant, overwhelming pressure to perform at work so I look good for the promotion, while also trying to keep my grades up in the certificate program so I actually qualify for the promotion. And I just... I feel like I'm failing at both because I can't keep all the plates spinning anymore. So, yeah, starting that program 15 months ago was a huge change, and it's definitely been the major stressor that's made all these memory and focus issues so much worse.
Have you noticed any changes in your physical health recently?

Physical health? Well, no, not really. I mean, I'm exhausted, obviously, but I think anyone would be with the schedule I just told you about. You know, working all day and then doing the classes at night, it just completely drains you. But as far as actual health problems, like getting sick or, I don't know, weird pains or anything like that? No. 

My immune system seems to be holding up, thankfully. I haven't even had so much as a cold this year, which is honestly kind of a miracle because usually when the seasons change, I get this terrible sinus thing that just knocks me out for a week. The office air conditioning is always blasting, and people come in coughing and touching the pens on my desk... but yeah, physically I'm fine. 

I do try to make sure I'm at least drinking enough water, even if my diet has kind of devolved into whatever I can grab from the vending machine or the drive-thru between work and my evening lectures. I know I should probably be eating better, maybe making salads or something, but who has the time to meal prep when you're forgetting to even buy the groceries in the first place, right? Like I was saying with the dry cleaning, if I can't even remember to pull into the store, I'm definitely not chopping vegetables. 

So, yeah, aside from just the general exhaustion of burning the candle at both ends and maybe not eating the greatest right now, my actual physical health hasn't changed at all. My blood pressure was totally fine at my last checkup, and I don't have any new physical issues. It really is just my brain that feels like it's completely malfunctioning.
Do you find yourself forgetting things even when you're relaxed and not feeling overwhelmed?

Relaxed? Gosh, um... I kind of have to search my memory for the last time I actually felt relaxed! With the 8 to 5 job and the evening classes, "relaxed" isn't exactly in my vocabulary right now. But... if I really think about it, like, maybe during the two-week break I had between the fall and spring semesters? 

During those two weeks, I didn't have any reading to do, no group projects to coordinate, and the office was actually pretty quiet because half the staff takes time off around the holidays. And you know what? No, I don't think I was forgetting things then. When I actually have real downtime, and I'm just... existing, without a million mental tabs open, my brain seems to function just fine. 

Like, during that break, I remembered to water my plants, I remembered to call my mom back—which she was thrilled about, because usually I see her name pop up on my phone, think "Oh, I'll call her after my lecture," and then completely blank on it for three days. But when the pressure is off and I'm not feeling completely buried under all the schedules and deadlines, I don't really have these memory blanks. 

It's like my brain only short-circuits when the system is overloaded. If I'm just sitting on the couch on a Sunday morning, drinking coffee and not worrying about whether I formatted the weekly executive report right or if I studied enough for my HR quiz, I don't find myself walking into a room and forgetting why I went in there. So I really think it's tied to just how much I'm trying to juggle. Because when the juggling stops, the dropping things stops too, if that makes sense? It's just that, right now, the juggling never really stops. Even when I try to take a bath or watch a show to unwind, I'm usually just making a mental list of what I have to do the next day, so I'm not *truly* relaxed anyway. But yeah, when I actually am? No, the forgetting doesn't really happen.
Do you find yourself forgetting steps or details when doing tasks you've done many times before?

Forgetting steps for things I've done a lot? Um... no, actually. No, I don't think so. Because, like I was saying earlier, I've been an admin assistant since I was basically eighteen, right out of high school. So the things I do every day, they're really like muscle memory at this point. 

Take the morning mail, for example. It sounds so simple, but there's a whole process to it that I've just perfected over the years. I get in, I unlock the filing cabinets, I sort the mail into three piles—urgent, standard, and junk. Then I have to date-stamp the standard mail, log the certified letters into the Excel tracker, and distribute them to the different departments before 9:30. I never forget to date-stamp them. I never forget to log them. It's just... boom, boom, boom, done. I don't even really have to think about it.

Or like, the weekly executive summary reports. I've been formatting those for our current office manager for, gosh, five years now? I know exactly what font she likes, I know she wants the margins at exactly 1.15 inches, I know she absolutely hates when the graphs get pushed to a separate page from the text. I don't forget those details because they're just hardwired into my brain at this point. I could probably do it with my eyes closed. 

It's really just the new stuff, or when I'm trying to hold too many things in my head at once, like the reading for my classes or trying to remember a one-off errand. But the routine stuff? The tasks I've done a hundred times? No, I'm actually really good at that. That's exactly why I know I'd be a great Office Manager, because I have all these systems completely locked down. If I was forgetting how to do my basic job, I wouldn't even be trying for the promotion, you know? It's just... when I step out of that routine, or when my brain gets yanked away by, say, suddenly remembering I have a human resources quiz at 7 PM, that's when things get messy. But the actual steps of my normal routine? No, I never miss a step there.
Do you have trouble remembering things that happened before you started experiencing these memory problems?

Things from before? Like, my long-term memory? Oh, no, not at all. My long-term memory is actually incredibly sharp. I can remember things from years ago with crystal clarity. 

Like, for instance, I can tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation—it was this pale yellow dress with little white daisies embroidered along the hem, and I had these terrible strappy sandals that gave me blisters before we even walked across the stage. I can remember the exact layout of my childhood bedroom, down to where my mom hung this weird macrame owl she bought at a craft fair in 1996. I can even remember the phone number of my best friend from middle school, 555-0198, even though I haven't dialed it in probably twenty years! 

And it's the same with work stuff from before this whole overwhelmed phase started. I can recall conversations I had with the old regional director three years ago, before he retired and moved to Florida. I remember he always used to ask for his coffee with exactly one and a half packets of Splenda, never two, because two was "too cloying," whatever that means. I remember the exact date we switched over our filing system from the old color-coded folders to the digital database—it was October 14th, four years ago, and it rained that whole week. 

So, no, anything that got filed away in my brain before I started taking these night classes and trying to juggle a million things at once... that stuff is totally secure. It's locked in the vault. It's really just the short-term stuff right now, the things that are happening while my brain is already at maximum capacity, that seem to just bounce right off. If you ask me what I had for dinner last night, I might have to really stop and think about it, but if you ask me about my tenth birthday party at the roller rink? I could tell you the entire playlist and what flavor the cake was. So the old memories are perfectly fine, it's just the new ones that aren't sticking.
Do you think your memory problems are triggered or made worse when you're under a lot of pressure to perform?

Pressure to perform? Um... you mean like, stage fright, or having a boss breathe down my neck? 

Actually, no, I haven't really noticed that being a trigger. It's kind of funny, because you'd think that would be the case, right? But if I'm, say, taking one of my HR exams for my evening classes—which is definitely high pressure because I absolutely have to keep a B average if I want the company to reimburse my tuition at the end of the semester—I don't sit there and blank out on what I studied. I actually do pretty well on the tests themselves. 

Or like at work, if my office manager is standing right over my desk waiting for me to pull a specific vendor contract for a sudden meeting with the regional VP, I don't suddenly forget how our filing system works or where I put the folder. If anything, when there's that kind of direct, immediate pressure to perform, it's almost like my brain snaps into focus. I get this little rush of adrenaline and I just handle it. I've always been pretty good in a pinch. Like just last month, our main copier jammed right before a massive quarterly review meeting, and I had to manually collate and staple thirty packets in about five minutes while three different executives were pacing around the lobby. High pressure, definitely! But I didn't forget what I was doing or miss any pages, I just got it done. 

So, no, I don't think it's the pressure to perform a specific task that makes me forget things. It's not performance anxiety or anything like that. Like I was saying before, it's really just the sheer volume of everything. It's when I have twenty completely mundane, low-pressure things floating around in my head—like remembering to buy cat food, and emailing the janitorial staff about the paper towels, and reading chapter four... that's when things slip through the cracks. But when all eyes are on me to do one important thing? No, I don't really have memory blanks then. The pressure almost helps, honestly. I know some people completely freeze up when they're put on the spot, like my sister, she completely bombs job interviews because of the pressure, but for me, that's really not when the forgetting happens.
Do you find it difficult to remember where you left off when you have to switch between different tasks or activities?

Switching tasks? And remembering where I left off? Um... no, actually, I don't really have a problem with that. Which is lucky, because being an administrative assistant, my entire day is basically just one long string of interruptions. If I couldn't remember where I left off, I'd never get a single thing done! 

Like, just to give you an idea of a normal Tuesday... I'll be right in the middle of typing up an email to our property management company because the air conditioning in the breakroom is making that horrible rattling noise again—which, honestly, happens every single summer like clockwork, you'd think they would just replace the main unit instead of sending the same maintenance guy, Gary, out to put a band-aid on it every July—but anyway, I'll be mid-sentence on that email, and then the multi-line phone will start ringing. And it's Brenda from accounting, and she absolutely needs me to track down a physical FedEx receipt from three weeks ago because her reconciliation is off by, like, four dollars and twelve cents. 

So I have to minimize my email, open up the shipping portal, physically get up and dig through the outgoing log binder... and then once I finally find it and give Brenda the tracking number, I sit back down at my desk. And when I open that draft back up? I know exactly what word I was about to type. I don't have to reread the whole email to figure out what I was doing. I just jump right back into complaining about the AC unit. 

Or if I'm in the middle of restocking the printer toner and someone walks into the lobby asking where the regional director's office is... I just stop, walk them down the hall, make some small talk about the traffic on I-95, and then walk right back to the copier and finish putting the cartridge in. I don't stand there wondering why my hands are covered in black ink, you know? I just pick right back up. 

I think because I've been at the front desk for so long, that kind of ping-ponging back and forth is just second nature to me now. It's my normal operating speed. It's really only when I'm trying to juggle all the new stuff, like the human resources classes and the studying on top of the normal life stuff, that my brain just sort of... hits a wall and drops things. But just switching from one normal task to another and going back again? No, I never lose my place with that. I'm actually really proud of how well I handle the front desk chaos, to be honest. If I couldn't bounce back from an interruption, our office manager would have replaced me years ago!
Do you find that you forget things more often when you're trying to do multiple things at the same time?

Doing multiple things at the same time? Um... no, not really. I mean, honestly, I'm practically the queen of multitasking. You kind of have to be when you're an administrative assistant, right? 

Like, just to give you an example, yesterday around noon I was on the phone with the Poland Spring water delivery guy—because they keep leaving the five-gallon jugs in the wrong hallway, right by the emergency exit, which is a massive fire hazard and I've told their dispatch office at least three times about it this month alone—but anyway, I was on the phone with him, while simultaneously typing up the minutes from the morning staff meeting, and eating my turkey and swiss sandwich. And I didn't forget what I was typing, and I didn't forget the point I was trying to make to the dispatcher, and I didn't accidentally type my lunch order into the meeting minutes! 

I actually kind of thrive when I have three different things going on at once. It's almost like a dance, you know? I can be transferring a call on line one, signing a clipboard for a UPS package with my right hand, and waving a visitor toward the waiting area with my left hand, all in the exact same ten seconds. My old boss, Mr. Henderson—the one who moved to Florida—he used to say I was like an octopus, just managing eight different things at once without even breaking a sweat. 

So no, I don't think doing things simultaneously is what makes me forget. The actual physical act of doing three things at once at my desk? I'm totally fine with that. I don't drop the ball when I'm actively juggling in the moment. It's really just... like I was saying before, it's having too many overarching responsibilities taking up space in my brain long-term, like knowing I have to read three chapters for my HR class by Thursday, and also remembering to pay the electric bill, and also remembering that the cat needs her flea medication. It's the background stuff that gets lost. But actively multitasking in the present moment? No, that doesn't seem to trigger the memory blanks at all. I've always been really good at doing a bunch of things at once.
Do you find yourself forgetting instructions or tasks that you've been given to complete?

Forgetting tasks? Yeah... yeah, actually, that's kind of the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you today. That is what finally made me ask for help. It's not the big, high-pressure stuff, like I was saying, and it's not when I'm actively multitasking. It's that I keep forgetting these little things that I normally handle without any issue at all. 

Like, returning phone calls. Someone will leave a message on my desk, maybe it's a vendor or maybe it's just my mom, and I tell myself I will call them right back as soon as I finish typing whatever I'm working on. And then... poof. It is completely gone from my brain until three days later when they call back annoyed, and I feel terrible because I usually pride myself on being so on top of communication.

Or turning in a registration form! I had this basic enrollment confirmation form for my evening HR classes a couple of weeks ago. I filled it out, I put it right in my purse, right in the front pocket so I wouldn't forget. And I walked right past the campus office building like four times that week and just completely forgot to actually take it out of my bag and hand it to the person at the desk. I didn't remember until they sent an automated warning email that I was going to be dropped from the roster. 

And stopping for an errand on the way home is honestly the worst one lately. I will remind myself all day at work that I have to stop at the store for my cat's flea medication or pick up milk. I will literally plan out the route in my head and tell myself not to forget. And then five o'clock hits, I get in my car, turn on the radio, get on the highway, and I just drive straight home on autopilot. I pull into my driveway, put the car in park, and realize I drove right past the shopping plaza without even a second thought. 

So, yes, it's those kinds of tasks. Just... everyday instructions and little things slipping through the cracks. It was driving me so crazy, and making me feel so scatterbrained, that I finally decided I had to come see a doctor about it.
Do you think that reducing your stress levels would help improve your memory?

Reduce my stress? Um... gosh, I mean, I really don't know. It's hard to even picture what that would look like right now, to be completely honest with you. Because when am I ever not stressed lately? Between managing the front desk, and the phones ringing off the hook, and dealing with Gary and the broken AC, and then trying to keep up with these evening HR classes... I feel like my baseline is just this constant, low-level hum of stress. 

My sister is actually always getting on my case about it. She’s always telling me that I need to decompress, that I need a spa day or whatever. And I did try that! Well, not a spa day, but a few weekends ago, I actually tried to just... do nothing. I didn't have any homework for my HR class because the professor had to push the syllabus back—which was a whole big drama because half the class had already bought the wrong textbook and they wouldn't let us return it, but anyway—I had a totally free Sunday. I slept in, I made myself a nice breakfast, I sat out on the patio with my coffee. It was total relaxation. Zero stress. 

But even then, on that completely chill Sunday where I had absolutely nothing to worry about, I still walked into the kitchen to get a refill of my coffee, got distracted by a dead leaf on my spider plant, ended up watering all the plants in the living room, and completely forgot about the coffee until I found it sitting on the counter three hours later, ice cold. 

So... I just don't know. I mean, maybe less stress would help? It sounds nice in theory, and I certainly wouldn't say no to a vacation! But since I seem to be dropping the ball and forgetting what I'm doing even when I'm just lounging around in my pajamas with literally nothing on my to-do list... I'm just not sure if the stress is the actual root of the memory problem, you know? I really couldn't say for sure.
Are you having difficulty remembering important details about your friends and family, such as their birthdays or anniversaries?

Birthdays and anniversaries? Oh, no. No, definitely not. Actually, I'm kind of the one who remembers everyone's everything in my family. 

I think it's because I've been doing administrative work for so long, you know? I just automatically log that kind of stuff. I live by my planner. My physical planner, I mean, not just the digital one on my phone—though I have that too, synced up with color-coding—but for family stuff, I have this big floral calendar I keep at home on the kitchen island. 

Like, my sister—the one who is always telling me to take a spa day—her anniversary was last month. Ten years with her husband, Mark. Well, they actually started dating twelve years ago, but married for ten. And I was the one who reminded our mom to send them a card! I actually bought the card for my mom while I was at CVS, brought it to her house, made her sign it, and put the stamp on it myself because otherwise she would have completely missed it. 

And birthdays? I never miss them. I know my nieces' birthdays, my best friend Sarah's birthday—which is Halloween, so that's a pretty easy one to remember, but still! I even remember my old boss Mr. Henderson's birthday, which is March 14th. Pi Day! He always brought in a pie instead of a cake, which I always thought was a fun little tradition. 

So, no, the important details about people, the big dates... those are totally locked in. It's so weird, right? Because like I was saying about the flea medication and returning those little phone messages at work, the everyday stuff just completely evaporates from my brain. But if you ask me when my parents' anniversary is, or when my nephew is graduating kindergarten, I can tell you the exact date, the time, and probably what kind of sheet cake we're ordering from Costco. I've always been the designated family calendar. So no, I haven't had any trouble with that at all.
Have you experienced any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your arms or legs?

Numbness or tingling? Oh, no. No, nothing like that. 

I mean, well... unless you count when my foot falls asleep because I've been sitting on it wrong at my desk for too long! But that's just because my office chair is honestly a complete nightmare. It's this cheap, squeaky mesh thing that the company bought in bulk like five years ago, and the cushion is completely shot. I keep asking Gary—he's the guy I mentioned who hasn't fixed the AC yet—to just let me order a new one from the supply catalog, or at least let me expense a proper ergonomic pillow, but there's always some excuse about the quarterly budget being frozen. 

So, because the chair is so uncomfortable, I have this terrible habit of tucking one leg under me while I'm typing up expense reports or answering emails. I know it's awful for my posture. My mom used to always yell at me for sitting like a pretzel when I was a teenager, but I still do it without even realizing it. And then I'll go to stand up to grab something off the printer and my foot will be totally dead, just full of pins and needles. 

But that goes away in a minute or two once I walk it off. Aside from that entirely self-inflicted thing, no, no random numbness or tingling out of nowhere. And definitely no weakness in my arms or legs either. They feel totally fine, just the normal amount of tired from, you know, running around the office all day. So no, definitely not experiencing any of that.
Do you have trouble remembering what happened yesterday or the day before?

Remembering what happened yesterday? Or the day before? Um, no, not really. I mean, I remember the big stuff, the actual events of the day, you know? Like, I can tell you exactly what happened yesterday. 

Yesterday was Tuesday, so it was our weekly staff meeting in the morning, which was... well, it was exactly as tedious as it always is. Or turning in a registration form! I had this basic enrollment confirmation form for my evening HR classes a couple of weeks ago. I didn't remember until they sent an automated warning email that I was going to be dropped from the roster.

I will literally plan out the route in my head and tell myself not to forget. And then five o'clock hits, I get in my car, turn on the radio, get on the highway, and I just drive straight home on autopilot. I pull into my driveway, put the car in park, and realize I drove right past the shopping plaza without even a second thought. 

So, yes, it's those kinds of tasks. Just... everyday instructions and little things slipping through the cracks. It was driving me so crazy, and making me feel so scatterbrained, that I finally decided I had to come see a doctor about it.

patient.answer:

I didn't have any homework for my HR class because the professor had to push the syllabus back—which was a whole big drama because half the class had already bought the wrong textbook and they wouldn't let us return it, but anyway—I had a totally free Sunday. I slept in, I made myself a nice breakfast, I sat out on the patio with my coffee. It was total relaxation. Zero stress. 

But even then, on that completely chill Sunday where I had absolutely nothing to worry about, I still walked into the kitchen to get a refill of my coffee, got distracted by a dead leaf on my spider plant, ended up watering all the plants in the living room, and completely forgot about the coffee until I found it sitting on the counter three hours later, ice cold. 

So... I just don't know. I mean, maybe less stress would help? It sounds nice in theory, and I certainly wouldn't say no to a vacation! But since I seem to be dropping the ball and forgetting what I'm doing even when I'm just lounging around in my pajamas with literally nothing on my to-do list... doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's memory issues are impacting their ability to maintain personal relationships

Birthdays and anniversaries? Oh, no. No, definitely not. Actually, I'm kind of the one who remembers everyone's everything in my family.

My physical planner, I mean, not just the digital one on my phone—though I have that too, synced up with color-coding—but for family stuff, I have this big floral calendar I keep at home on the kitchen island. 

Like, my sister—the one who is always telling me to take a spa day—her anniversary was last month. Ten years with her husband, Mark. Well, they actually started dating twelve years ago, but married for ten. And I was the one who reminded our mom to send them a card! I actually bought the card for my mom while I was at CVS, brought it to her house, made her sign it, and put the stamp on it myself because otherwise she would have completely missed it.

I even remember my old boss Mr. Henderson's birthday, which is March 14th. Pi Day! He always brought in a pie instead of a cake, which I always thought was a fun little tradition. 

So, no, the important details about people, the big dates... those are totally locked in. It's so weird, right? Because like I was saying about the flea medication and returning those little phone messages at work, the everyday stuff just completely evaporates from my brain. But if you ask me when my parents' anniversary is, or when my nephew is graduating kindergarten, I can tell you the exact date, the time, and probably what kind of sheet cake we're ordering from Costco. Remembering what happened yesterday? Or the day before? Um, no, not really. I mean, I remember the big stuff, the actual events of the day, you know? Like, I can tell you exactly what happened yesterday.

And then after the meeting, I had my usual lunch—I always bring a turkey sandwich on Tuesdays because I roast a turkey breast on Sundays, and Tuesday is when it's still good but I need to finish it before it gets weird. And then the day before yesterday, Monday, was just... Monday. You know how Mondays are. The phones were crazy because everyone was calling about things they thought of over the weekend. Oh! And the delivery guy for the water cooler brought the wrong jugs. He brought the ones with the little spigot on the bottom instead of the ones that go on top of the machine, so I had to call the company and get that sorted out, which took forever because their customer service line just puts you on hold with this awful smooth jazz music. 

So, yeah, I can definitely remember what happened, like, the actual narrative of my day. I know what I did, where I went, who I talked to. It's not like my days are just a blank slate or anything. But as far as just knowing what happened yesterday or the day before? No, I don't have any trouble with that. I can give you a full play-by-play if you really want it! patient.answer:
Conversations earlier in the day? Um, no, I wouldn't say I have trouble remembering them. I mean, if I have a conversation with someone, I know it happened and I know what we talked about. 

Like this morning, before I came here, I was talking to the receptionist at my dentist's office—I had to call to reschedule a cleaning because they double-booked me with my car inspection, which is a whole other frustrating story because I specifically told them I needed a Tuesday afternoon, but anyway—I remember exactly what she said. So, I remember all of that. The actual content of the conversation, the people, what we were discussing—that all stays in my head just fine. I don't forget that I spoke to someone or what the gist of it was. 

Now, if you ask me if I remember every single word, like a transcript? Well, no, but nobody does that, right? But the actual conversation itself, no, I don't lose those.

But the conversation itself? No, I don't forget those. If I talk to someone at 9 AM, by 3 PM I still know exactly what we talked about.
